title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential BST insertion (unbalanced) versus divide-and-conquer construction using the middle element as root.

content.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums sorted in ascending order (with unique values), convert it to a height-balanced binary search tree.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, sorted ascending, unique values"],["Output","A height-balanced BST containing the same values"],["Goal","Build the tree by always picking the middle element as root, guaranteeing balance"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Sorted array\" plus \"build a height-balanced BST\"","Divide and conquer: pick the middle element as root, recurse on both halves"],["Balance guarantee needed","The middle element always splits the remaining range into two nearly equal halves"]]}

blocks.text: Choosing the middle element of the sorted array as the root automatically satisfies the BST property (everything before is smaller, everything after is larger) and, applied recursively, guarantees the tree stays balanced, since each split divides the remaining elements as evenly as possible.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building a Balanced Organization Chart from a Sorted Seniority List
blocks.text: Picture building a balanced hierarchy from a sorted list of employees by seniority, picking the middle-seniority employee as the top of each branch, then recursively doing the same for those above and below them. This naturally keeps the hierarchy shallow and balanced.

blocks.caption: Picking the middle element as root and recursing on both halves keeps the tree height-balanced

blocks.text: Result (preorder): 0 -10 null -3 null null 5 null 9 null null. Root 0, left subtree from [-10,-3], right subtree from [5,9].

Before inserting values one by one (which would create a skewed tree for sorted input), notice picking the middle element as root at every level guarantees balance directly, since the same divide-and-conquer idea as binary search applies to tree construction.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Inserting sorted values sequentially into a plain BST produces a completely skewed, linked-list-shaped tree.

Observation 2: Instead, picking the MIDDLE element of the current range as root guarantees roughly equal halves remain for the left and right subtrees.

Observation 3: Applying this same rule recursively to each half builds a tree where every subtree is balanced by construction.

Observation 4: This mirrors the classic binary search "pick the middle" idea, but building a tree instead of searching one.
This leads to recursively building the tree: pick the middle index of the current range as root, recurse on the left sub-range for the left child, recurse on the right sub-range for the right child.
Insert each value from the sorted array into a BST one at a time, using standard BST insertion, without any balancing.
Why the code is written this way

items: Standard BST insertion is simple and produces a valid BST.
Inserting sorted values in order always appends to the same side, giving O(n) height instead of the required O(log n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case, inserting into a growing skewed tree.
Space: O(n), but tree height O(n) (not balanced).
Limitation: this fails the height-balanced requirement; explicitly picking the middle element as root guarantees O(log n) height.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since the array is already sorted, choosing the MIDDLE index as root at every recursive level guarantees the two halves differ in size by at most one, bounding the resulting tree's height at O(log n), directly satisfying the height-balanced requirement.
Recursively build: for a range [l, r], pick mid = (l+r)/2 as root, recurse on [l, mid-1] for the left child and [mid+1, r] for the right child.

Since the data is sorted, choosing the middle index as root at every level automatically satisfies the BST property and guarantees the two halves differ in size by at most one, bounding the resulting tree's height at O(log n), the height-balanced requirement.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), visiting each element once.
Space: O(n) for the tree, O(log n) recursion depth.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "build a balanced structure from sorted data", think: divide and conquer, middle becomes root, recurse on both halves.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sequential insertion costs O(n squared) and produces an unbalanced tree; the middle-as-root approach costs O(n) and guarantees O(log n) height.

items: Pattern: divide and conquer, picking the middle element as root at every recursive level.
Core Idea: middle index becomes root; left half becomes left subtree, right half becomes right subtree, recursively.
Time: O(n squared) for sequential insertion, O(n) for the divide-and-conquer approach.
Space: O(n) for both, but only the divide-and-conquer approach guarantees O(log n) height.
Most Important Observation: the middle element split keeps the tree height-balanced at every level.
Interview Difficulty: a direct, accessible application of the binary-search "pick the middle" idea.
One line memory trick: middle becomes root; recurse left half and right half.
